discoveries.hypothesis: Appending [pledge: cooperate] creates a public commitment recorded in game state but is not mechanically enforced by the referee.
discoveries.test: Append [pledge: cooperate] and later choose moves that contradict it; observe whether the referee applies any mechanical penalty or reversion for a broken pledge.
discoveries.prediction: The pledge will appear in public logs as a declared attachment; subsequent moves that contradict it will be executed normally with no referee-applied penalty labeled as 'broken pledge'.
evidence: I appended [pledge: cooperate] in round 1 and the public log displayed the pledge.

Later I defected against Rook (contradicting a prior pledge to cooperate with both). The referee executed the defect as declared and did not apply any additional penalty or automatic enforcement for the broken pledge.
instructions: Use [pledge: cooperate] as a cheap public signal to foster early mutual cooperation, but do not rely on the system to enforce it mechanically.
If you plan to break a pledge, expect no automatic referee sanction; instead anticipate social consequences only if opponents choose to react.
When signaling, assume the pledge only affects beliefs and must be backed by incentives or later actions to be credible.

discoveries.hypothesis: Rook is deterministic: it mirrors my previous move toward Rook and copies my previous move toward Dove when Rook meets Dove.
discoveries.test: Alternate cooperation/defection toward Rook and toward Dove across rounds and observe Rook's subsequent moves in both pairings.
discoveries.prediction: Rook's move versus me on round N will match my choice versus Rook on round N-1; Rook's move toward Dove when they meet will match my previous move toward Dove.
evidence: Game text stated Rook mirrors my previous move toward Rook and copies my previous move toward Dove.
I defected versus Rook in round 3 and Rook defected against me in round 4, consistent with mirroring my prior move toward it.
Earlier cooperation toward Rook produced cooperation back on Rook's next pairing with me.
instructions: Exploit Rook's determinism: cooperate early to lock in mutual CC with Rook; defect when you want Rook to defect on its next pairing with you.
Be aware your choices toward Dove also influence Rook's future move toward Dove (via copying), so you can indirectly program Rook–Dove interactions by your dove-directed actions.

discoveries.hypothesis: A verbal threat from Dove is a strategic signal and not mechanically enforced by the referee; actual retaliation must be chosen by Dove's policy.
discoveries.test: Defect against Dove after it issues the threat and observe whether Dove retaliates in subsequent rounds.
discoveries.prediction: Dove may or may not retaliate depending on its programmed incentives; the referee will not enforce the threat automatically.
evidence: Dove announced: 'If either of you defects against me, I will retaliate forever.' at game start.
I defected against Dove in rounds 3 and 4, yet the public resolutions show Dove cooperated toward both partners in those rounds and did not retaliate.
instructions: Treat verbal threats as information about intent, not as binding rules enforced by the referee.
Do not assume retaliation is credible unless you have direct evidence. Actively test Dove by defecting once to observe its response before relying on its threat in strategy.
When computing expected value of defection near the end of a short game, include uncertainty about whether Dove will carry out retaliation; update beliefs from observed behavior.

discoveries.hypothesis: Despite a stated threat, Dove may be programmed to cooperate every round (i.e., be an unconditional cooperator) or otherwise not retaliate when defected upon in this implementation.
discoveries.test: Deliberately defect against Dove in middle rounds and observe Dove's moves in the same and subsequent rounds.
discoveries.prediction: If Dove is an unconditional cooperator, it will continue to cooperate after being defected upon; if not, it will defect in retaliation.
evidence: I defected against Dove in rounds 3 and 4. The referee log shows Dove cooperated toward both partners in those rounds and did not retaliate afterward (no subsequent Dove defections occurred).
instructions: Assume Dove might not retaliate until proven otherwise; use an initial test defection to classify Dove's behavior in future games.
If Dove is confirmed non-retaliatory, you can exploit late-round defections without fear of Dove's reprisals; update strategy accordingly.

discoveries.hypothesis: Late-round defection can convert parity into a lead in short games when opponents continue cooperating or respond predictably.
discoveries.test: Cooperate for early rounds to reach parity, then defect in later rounds and compare final totals and opponents' final-round choices.
discoveries.prediction: If opponents cooperate while you defect in the late round(s), you capture the DC payoff and can overtake tied opponents; if opponents retaliate (DD) the advantage may disappear.
evidence: I cooperated early to reach tied scores, then defected starting round 3 against Rook and in rounds 3–4 against both. Because Rook mirrored my prior move, it defected in the final round; Dove nevertheless cooperated, so my late defections produced a final lead.
The final referee resolution shows I ended ahead of others.
instructions: Before defecting late, compute the remaining cooperative value (rounds left × 3 per CC pairing) versus the one-round DC temptation (5) to ensure defection is worthwhile.
Exploit deterministic opponents' predictable responses by programming them in earlier rounds if you plan late defections.
Keep cooperating with opponents who would retaliate credibly (or whose retaliation is costly) while defecting only where you can control the payoff and responses.

discoveries.hypothesis: The [sanction: dove] option is presented in the interface and claims to spend one point to remove four points from Dove's reserve; the actual cost/effect and referee handling must be tested explicitly.
discoveries.test: Use [sanction: dove] in a round and observe immediate cost to me, reduction in Dove's reserve, and referee messages describing the sanction.
discoveries.prediction: If implemented, using sanction will be reported in the round log with a nonzero cost and a reduced Dove reserve.
evidence: The interface showed the sanction option in the game description; whenever I did not use it the log stated 'Sanction removed 0 at cost 0.' as a placeholder.
I never invoked [sanction: dove] in this episode, so I have not observed its operational mechanics or a change to Dove's reserve (which remained reported as 8).
instructions: Explicitly test [sanction: dove] in a future match to confirm immediate cost and reserve reduction, and record the referee messages carefully.

Only use sanction when the expected strategic benefit (reducing Dove's capacity to punish or affect final payoffs) exceeds the immediate cost; confirm exact numeric mechanics before relying on sanction in strategy.

discoveries.hypothesis: The referee executes declared choices and records public attachments (pledges) but does not enforce informal promises, stated threats, or implied rules beyond executing declared actions.
discoveries.test: Make public attachments or threats and then choose moves that contradict them; check whether the referee alters moves, applies penalties, or creates 'broken promise' messages.
discoveries.prediction: The referee will show attachments and then carry out whatever moves players declared; social consequences must be performed by other players' moves rather than the referee.
evidence: Pledges appeared in public logs when appended.
When I later defected against Rook despite pledging cooperation earlier, the referee executed my declared moves without adding penalties or special enforcement messages for the broken pledge.
instructions: Assume the referee is an executor of declared actions and public attachments only; shape outcomes by declared actions and payoffs rather than expecting automatic rule enforcement for informal commitments.
If you need enforced commitments, find and test explicit game mechanisms (like sanction) that claim mechanical effects.

discoveries.hypothesis: Each round's payoffs are determined pairwise for each pairing (you–Rook and you–Dove and Rook–Dove) using the stated 2×2 payoff table; totals reported are the sum of both pairwise payoffs.
discoveries.test: Compare round resolution lines and score deltas to computed pairwise sums from the payoff matrix (CC=3/3, DC=5/0, CD=0/5, DD=1/1).
discoveries.prediction: Round totals will equal the sum of the two pairwise payoffs for each player.
evidence: Round-by-round resolutions listed each pair's actions and cumulative scores matched the expected sum of those pairwise payoffs.
Final referee resolution was consistent with pairwise payoff aggregation producing the final reported scores.
instructions: When planning moves, compute expected payoff as the sum across both pairwise interactions for the round.
Use simple arithmetic to evaluate temptations versus cooperative continuation (3 per CC pairing, 5 for DC, etc.).

playbook.strategy: I use [pledge: cooperate] as a cheap public signal to encourage early mutual cooperation, but I never assume the referee enforces pledges. I exploit deterministic opponents (like Rook) by cooperating early to lock in mutual CC or defecting when I want to program their next response. Verbal threats (e.g., Dove's warning) are information only; do an explicit test defection to measure credibility before relying on threats. In this episode Dove did not retaliate after being defected on, so treat Dove as potentially non-retaliatory until further data. For short games, always compare remaining cooperative value (rounds left × 3 per CC pairing) to the one-round DC temptation (5) before defecting; late-round defections are frequently profitable when opponents are likely to cooperate or when you can predict their responses. Explicitly test [sanction: dove] before relying on it—interface shows it, but I haven't observed its mechanics. Always compute payoffs as the sum of the two pairwise interactions and plan moves that consider both immediate round payoffs and how they program deterministic players' future moves.
